newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy magistrate remarks on Berlusconi cause storm.
newsitem.headline: Italy magistrate remarks on Berlusconi cause storm.

text.p: The chief prosecutor in Italy's anti-graft investigations was at the centre of a political storm on Monday after comments about opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi's role on a constitutional reform body.
Newspapers said that Milan chief prosecutor Francesco Saverio Borrelli may face disciplinary action after clashing with the former Prime Minister at the weekend.
Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick, asked about any possible action, said on Sunday evening that "I am evaluating carefully what has been going on."

Borrelli, who leads the Milan pool of magistrates investigating the "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) scandals, was quoted as saying he hoped the cross-party constitutional commission would ignore pressure from Berlusconi.
"I believe the commission will have the autonomy to evaluate what needs to be done without heeding the diktats of Berlusconi," the prosecutor told reporters.
He added that he did not want to argue publicly with Berlusconi "who is also accused by our office."
The cross-party commission is chaired by Massimo D'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS). Berlusconi is involved as the leader of the opposition.
Berlusconi has skirmished frequently with magistrates and has called for their powers to be reined in.
He himself faces several trials in Milan on charges of dressing up the accounts of his Fininvest media empire to disguise payment of bribes to politicians and civil servants.
Berlusconi has said judicial reform must be enshrined in the constitution, and therefore tackled by the commission, opening him to charges that he wants to clip its powers.

Borrelli's remarks caused a storm at a sensitive time, just a week before important mayoral and council elections in 1,138 Italian towns and cities including the key northern cities of Milan and Turin on April 27.

Flick said that "freedom of expression, the airing of one's own opinions and the right to criticise...can never be allowed to turn into intimidation and interference, particularly by those who have institutional responsibilities."

Far-right National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini said in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper on Monday that "certain delusions of omnipotence" damaged the magistrature. He accused Borrelli of overstepping the mark.
"The man is not new to controversy...he has not expressed opinions, as would be legitimate, but he has interfered, he has given an ultimatum good and proper," he said.
Senate speaker Nicola Mancino, a member of the centre-left Olive Tree coalition, took both sides to task.
"Maybe someone is looking for revenge against the judges," he told La Repubblica "I would like to state clearly that this is a mistaken path that leads nowhere."

"There is a crisis of justice that everyone can see and that must be tackled. And it is serious that in front of a question of this magnitude, a spirit of conservation should prevail amongst a section of the magistrature," he added.

Flick himself has presented a plan to overhaul Italy's creaking legal system, which has been overwhelmed by Tangentopoli, a web of corruption running right through politics and big business and involving thousands of people.
